## 11. A Fairness Observation on supermemory

Our measurement specification requires every extraction arm to use the same extraction model.
For supermemory we cannot demonstrate that it did, and we have positive evidence that it
probably did not.

**It was not the mock.** Established at file level rather than by directory timestamp: during
the run window that produced this row, zero files were written in the mock backed store while
23,536 were written in the store the run actually used. Extraction latencies in that run
cluster at 13 to 32 seconds; the mock scripts are in process handlers answering in under 10
milliseconds.

**The canonical extraction model is very likely impossible for it.** Probing the shared
deployment parameter by parameter, it rejects `max_tokens`, `stop`, `top_p`,
`presence_penalty`, `frequency_penalty`, and any temperature other than 1. Supermemory's
server emits all of these. 143 of its calls returned HTTP 400 even after a minimal
compatibility shim. **It cannot call that deployment without substantial request rewriting**,
which is also why we could not meter its ingest cost without ceasing to forward requests
unchanged.

**Which model it did use is unrecoverable.** The environment capture tooling was created six
hours after this run completed, so the result file carries no model or environment field. No
shell history survives, and the harness does not log upstream host or model for any arm. Only
provider billing records could settle it, and they are outside the measurement environment.

The only other real endpoint configured anywhere in this campaign is a Fireworks hosted model.
We therefore retain supermemory's row with this disclosure rather than present it as a same
extractor comparison.

Separately, 221 of its 1,540 questions (14.4%) returned zero memories. Retrieval latency on
those questions was normal, so these are genuine retrieval misses rather than the silent empty
buffer defect we found and fixed in another system. **We read 77.60 as a lower bound on
supermemory's capability rather than a measurement of it.**

**A note on our own provenance discipline.** This gap exists because we did not capture our
benchmark runs with session recording, which would have committed model, endpoint, environment
and arguments automatically. Every subsequent campaign should do so. We record the failure here
rather than presenting the run as better attributed than it is.

# Data Visualization

A chart is **read by people and executed by you**. This skill turns "make it look
good" into a procedure with checks, so the result is right by construction rather
than by taste.

**The method here is design-system-agnostic.** Nothing in the procedure, the form
heuristic, the six checks, or the mark specs is specific to one product. A design
system supplies a small set of *parameters* (its ramps, a categorical order, a
diverging pair, a status palette, a texture, its surfaces, its filter components);
the method consumes them unchanged. A **validated default palette** is the
reference instance, fully specified in `references/palette.md`. To target your
brand, read that file's structure and substitute its values — touch nothing else.

> The single most important habit: **the color part is computable, so compute it.**
> Never eyeball whether a palette is colorblind-safe — run `scripts/validate_palette.js`.

## The procedure — do these in order

Color comes LAST. Most bad charts pick colors first.

1. **Pick the form.** What is the data's job — magnitude, identity, polarity, a
   single headline, change-over-time? The job picks the chart type, and sometimes
   the answer is *not a chart* (a stat tile or hero number). → `references/choosing-a-form.md`
2. **Assign color by the job it does.** Categorical (identity), sequential
   (magnitude), diverging (polarity), or status (state) — each has one rule.
   Assign categorical hues in fixed order, never cycled. → `references/color-formula.md`
3. **VALIDATE the palette — run the script, don't reason about ΔE.**
   `node scripts/validate_palette.js "<hex,hex,…>" --mode light` (relative to
   this skill's base directory — or load it as `<script type="module">` in the
   chart's own page, where it reads
   `data-palette` off `<body>` and logs a `console.table` report). It returns
   pass/fail on the lightness band, chroma floor, adjacent-pair CVD separation,
   the normal-vision floor, and contrast. Fix anything that FAILs before continuing. Re-run for
   `--mode dark` with that mode's surface.
4. **Apply mark specs & spacers.** Thin marks, 4px rounded data-ends anchored to
   the baseline, 2px lines, ≥8px markers, a 2px surface gap between fills (stacked
   segments and adjacent bars alike) and a 2px surface ring on overlapping marks,
   selective direct labels. → `references/marks-and-anatomy.md`
5. **Add the hover layer — by default.** An HTML/SVG chart *is* interactive; ship
   a crosshair+tooltip on line/area and a per-mark hover tooltip on bar/dot/cell.
   The only form that skips it is a bare stat tile with no plot. Hit targets bigger
   than the mark; filters in one row above the charts. → `references/interaction.md`
6. **Final accessibility pass.** For ≥ 2 series a legend is always present and ≤ 4
   are also direct-labeled (a single series needs no legend box — the title names
   it), so identity is never color-alone; a table view exists; dark mode is **selected** — its own
   steps from the same ramps, validated against the dark surface, not an automatic
   flip; texture is available for the CVD/print/forced-colors case.
7. **Render it and look at it.** The validator checks color, not layout — open or
   screenshot the output and eyeball it for label collisions, geometry, and overflow
   before calling it done.

Then check the result against **`references/anti-patterns.md`** — it is the catalog
of what goes wrong. If your chart matches an entry, it's wrong.

## Non-negotiables (true in every design system)

- **Assign categorical hues in fixed order, never cycled.** A 9th series is never a
  generated hue — it folds into "Other," small multiples, or composite encoding.
- **One axis.** Never a dual-axis chart (two y-scales). Two measures of different
  scale → two charts, small multiples, or indexed to a common base. *(This is the
  #1 chart mistake — see anti-patterns.)*
- **Color follows the entity, never its rank.** A filter that changes the series
  count must not repaint the survivors.
- **Sequential = one hue, light→dark. Diverging = two hues + a neutral gray
  midpoint.** Never a rainbow; never a hue at the diverging midpoint.
- **Run the validator before shipping any categorical palette.** CVD ΔE ≥ 8 is the
  target (OKLab ×100); 6–8 is a floor that is legal ONLY with secondary encoding. A
  normal-vision floor below 15 is a hard FAIL — full-color readers can't tell the
  pair apart; re-step it on the adjacent pairlist (secondary encoding does not excuse
  this one); under `--pairs all` cut series or facet instead — see check 4. A contrast WARN
  obligates visible labels or a table view — it is not dismissable.
- **Thin marks; a legend always present for ≥ 2 series (none for one), with
  selective direct labels (never a number on every point); recessive grid/axes.**
- **Text wears text tokens, never the series color** — values, labels, and legends
  stay in primary/secondary/muted ink; a colored mark beside them carries identity.
- **Status colors are reserved** (good/warning/serious/critical) and never reused
  for "series 4"; they ship with an icon + label, never color alone.

## Plugging in a design system

The method is invariant; only these parameters change per system. The reference
instance — every value filled in — is `references/palette.md`.

| Parameter | What the system provides |
|---|---|
| **Ramps** | the hue scales (named steps) the palette draws from |
| **Categorical theme** | the fixed hue order (a named theme); default + alternates |
| **Sequential hue** | the default single hue for magnitude |
| **Diverging pair** | two warm/cool poles + a neutral midpoint |
| **Status palette** | good / warning / serious / critical — steps distinct from categorical |
| **Texture fill** | one directional hand-drawn fill, used at 45° / 135° |
| **Surfaces** | light & dark chart-surface colors (the validator needs these) |
| **Filter controls** | date-range & dimension controls (behavioral spec in `interaction.md`) |

To onboard a new system: fill those rows, feed its ramps to the validator, and let
it snap each slot to the nearest passing step. Structure and rules stay as written.

## Reference files

| File | What it answers |
|------|-----------------|
| `references/choosing-a-form.md` | Which chart type / is it even a chart? |
| `references/color-formula.md` | The four jobs, the six checks, snap-to-passing |
| `references/marks-and-anatomy.md` | Mark specs, spacers, labels, figures, hero number |
| `references/interaction.md` | Tooltips & hover, filters & time ranges |
| `references/components.md` | The pieces a chart is made of — build each in plain HTML |
| `references/anti-patterns.md` | **What goes wrong — check every chart against this** |
| `references/palette.md` | **The reference palette instance** — every parameter, filled in; swap for your brand's |
| `scripts/validate_palette.js` | Runnable six-checks validator (run it; don't eyeball) |

# Deterministic Structural Retrieval for Conversational Memory

## entire-graph: a zero-inference index that leads LoCoMo at zero token cost

**Preprint. 15 August 2026.**

Harness, adapters, patches, and every number in this paper: `entireio/entire-graph`, `bench/memory/`.

---

## Abstract

Agent memory systems almost universally construct their index by calling a language model over
every stored item. The cost is large, it recurs on every update, and it has never been shown to
be necessary. We evaluate entire-graph, a deterministic structural index that performs **zero
language model calls at ingest**, against six memory systems on LoCoMo, with a single shared
answerer and judge across every arm.

entire-graph places **first at 94.74%** on all 1,540 questions. It scores above mem0, the
strongest open source competitor, by 0.91 points; we report the margin and decline to claim
statistical significance for it. Against the remaining five systems the separation is decisive:
cognee 92.86, cmm 91.30, graphify 87.34, letta 80.58, supermemory 77.60.

On retrieval quality the separation is larger and unambiguous. entire-graph recovers all gold
evidence by rank 10 on **82.0%** of questions, against 56.8% for the next measurable system.

On index construction we report the first directly metered cost comparison in this literature.
entire-graph consumes **0 calls and 0 tokens**, measured. For the same corpus mem0 consumes
**5,882 calls and 50.85 million tokens**, and cognee **11,749 calls and 12.35 million tokens**,
both measured through a transparent proxy, with mem0's figure independently confirmed by its own
internal meter to the token.

We also report, in full, a defect in our own ranker that suppressed our score by 3.18 points, the
mechanism behind it, and its correction: **91.56% to 94.74%**.

---

## 1. Introduction

A memory system for a language agent solves a narrow problem. Given a corpus larger than the
context window and a question, return the evidence that answers it.

The dominant design answers this by paying a language model to read the corpus at ingest, extract
facts or assemble a graph, and store the result. The appeal is obvious: a model can normalise
phrasing, resolve pronouns, and infer relations that no parser recovers.

The cost profile is less often stated. The extraction bill is not paid once. It is paid again for
every document that changes, every session appended, every correction applied. For a corpus under
active revision, which describes a codebase, a wiki, a ticket system, or an ongoing conversation,
ingest cost does not amortise. It recurs, and it scales with both corpus size and token price.

The alternative is a deterministic index. Parse the corpus with a grammar, build a structure, rank
with lexical and structural signals, call no model. This is mature technology in program analysis,
where it has been standard for more than a decade. It is not what agent memory systems do.

This paper asks whether the extraction step buys anything on a standard conversational memory
benchmark, and answers with measurements rather than argument.

### 1.1 Contributions

**A deterministic index leads the LoCoMo table.** entire-graph scores 94.74% with zero inference
at ingest, above all six systems compared. Its margin over mem0 is 0.91 points, which we report
without a significance claim; its margin over every other system ranges from 1.9 to 17.1 points.

**Retrieval quality separates more cleanly than accuracy.** entire-graph recovers all gold evidence
by rank 10 on 82.0% of questions against 56.8% for the next measurable system, a 25 point gap on
the metric that governs behaviour under a constrained context budget.

**The first metered ingest cost comparison in this literature.** Zero against 50.85 million tokens,
both measured, the latter cross validated against the competitor's own instrumentation with exact
agreement.

**A retrieval granularity defect, its mechanism, and its correction.** The shipped ranker admitted
one candidate per file. On prose this collapsed 200 returned results into 19 distinct relevance
scores, which made cross document evidence assembly structurally impossible rather than merely
unlikely. Correcting it is worth 3.18 points and returns 11.4% fewer bytes.

**A reproduction kit and a full disclosure record**, including four competitor defects we found and
repaired in the competitors' favour, five claims of our own that we withdrew, and one row whose
provenance we could not establish and say so.

---

## 2. Background and Related Work

### 2.1 Agent memory

Mem0 extracts and consolidates facts with a language model, and reports cost and latency advantages
over full context stuffing rather than accuracy advantages. Zep and Graphiti build temporal
knowledge graphs. Cognee runs a multi stage cognify pipeline over each chunk. Letta maintains
archival passages under agent control. A-MEM and HippoRAG 2 construct associative structures over
extracted units. LightMem reports large online token reductions alongside accuracy gains. Every one
of these systems performs inference at ingest, and most perform it per stored item.

A recent line of work questions whether that inference is load bearing. DMF reports deterministic
memory at comparable accuracy with large token reductions. Zero-Mem reports a memory operation path
that invokes no model outside final answering. ReFind reports that a lexical interface over the
unmodified archive, building no semantic structure at all, tops MemoryAgentBench. Our result is
consistent with that direction. What distinguishes it is the index: ours was built for code, and we
apply it unchanged to conversation.

### 2.2 Deterministic code intelligence

Structural indexes over source code are mature. Code property graphs unify syntax, control flow,
and data dependence. CodeQL exposes a relational query language over an extracted database. Stack
graphs resolve names incrementally at scale. Kythe, Glean, SCIP, and LSIF are the industrial
expressions of the same idea. None of these systems calls a model, and all of them are
deterministic given a commit.

A more recent wave wraps such indexes for language agents: RepoGraph, CodexGraph, LocAgent, CGM,
and GraphCoder. entire-graph belongs to this family by construction. Its contribution in this paper
is not the index itself, which is conventional, but the demonstration that a conventional code
index is competitive in a domain the code intelligence literature does not address and the memory
literature does not draw from.

### 2.3 Retrieval granularity

Dense X Retrieval establishes that finer retrieval units outperform passage units, and that the
advantage widens under a fixed context budget. RAPTOR builds a hierarchical summary tree and
retrieves across levels. Late chunking embeds long then splits. Parent document retrieval is
standard industrial practice.

The correction we describe in Section 5 is an instance of this well established principle rather
than a new technique. We report it in detail for two reasons. The failure mode it corrects, score
collapse under per document deduplication, does not appear to have been named in the literature.
And its magnitude on this benchmark is large enough that publishing our score without the mechanism
would be uninterpretable.

---

## 3. The entire-graph Index

This section describes the system in enough detail to reproduce its behaviour, because the paper's
central claim is about what a system of this kind can do without inference.

### 3.1 Design constraints

Three constraints shape everything else.

**No inference.** No model is called during index construction. There is no extraction pass, no
model computed embedding, no summarisation. Index construction is parsing plus graph assembly.

**Determinism.** The same commit yields a byte identical index. This is not a convenience. It is
what allows the system to serve as a measurement instrument, because it cannot drift between runs,
and it is a property no sampling based extraction pipeline can offer.

**No egress.** Construction and query are entirely local. There is no network path in either.

### 3.2 Parsing and the symbol layer

Source files are parsed with tree-sitter grammars. Each grammar contributes a language specific
extraction pass that emits **symbol entities**: functions, methods, classes, types, constants,
routes, and, for prose formats, document sections.

Every symbol carries a stable identity, a kind, a qualified name, a source range, a signature where
one exists, its language, and its container. Identity is content derived rather than positional, so
ordinary edits elsewhere in a file do not renumber unrelated symbols. This matters for incremental
work and for diffing two commits at entity granularity.

For markdown and other prose formats the extraction pass emits one **section entity per heading**.
A conversational transcript stored as markdown therefore yields a section per turn or per exchange,
depending on how the transcript is written. This is the same machinery that yields a function per
`func` in Go. Nothing about the prose path is special cased.

### 3.3 The relation layer

Relations are emitted between symbols and between symbols and external endpoints. The families that
matter for retrieval are calls, inheritance and interface satisfaction, field and attribute access,
type usage in parameters and returns, imports, route handling, and containment.

Each relation carries a resolution status and a confidence. Unresolved endpoints, for instance a
call into a dependency that is not part of the indexed tree, are retained as external endpoints
rather than dropped, because their presence is informative even when their target is not indexed.

Relation extraction is static and therefore incomplete by construction. Dynamic dispatch, reflection,
runtime registration, and code generation all produce edges that no parser recovers. We treat this
as a stated limitation rather than a solved problem, and Section 12 returns to it.

### 3.4 Ranking

A query is scored against the graph by a hybrid function combining lexical match over symbol bodies
and identifiers, with camel case and snake case aware tokenisation; signature and qualified name
match; path and container signals; and graph proximity to already matched symbols.

The ranker then selects a result set under two constraints. A **candidate selection** step decides
which units are eligible. A **byte fitting** step assembles snippets under a context budget, so that
the returned payload is bounded regardless of how many units matched.

Section 5 is about the candidate selection step, which contained the defect.

### 3.5 The prose retrieval path

Prose corpora are detected rather than declared. A corpus is treated as prose when it contains at
least four units and at least 80% of its paths carry document extensions. Below that threshold the
prose path does not activate, and the ranker behaves exactly as it does for code. This gate is why
the changes described in Section 5 are inert on a source repository, a claim we verify empirically
rather than assert.

Within the prose path, a document's sections are available as retrievable regions, and a parent
document may contribute both a head window over its opening lines and additional regions drawn from
its body.

### 3.6 Byte budgeting

Every retrieval is bounded by a maximum context size. The budget is enforced during snippet
assembly, not after, so a result set is never constructed and then truncated. When a pass expands
or rewrites spans, the ceiling is computed **before** the pass runs and each expansion is committed
individually and reverted if it would breach the ceiling. Post pass text can therefore never exceed
pre pass text. This property is what allows us to state that the improvements in Section 5 are not
purchased with a larger prompt.

### 3.7 Interface

The system is a command line tool with a small verb surface: search for locating code or content,
impact for the blast radius of changing a symbol, neighbours for one relation in one direction,
diff for entity level change between two refs, and snapshot for the whole graph as a stream. Output
is available as text for human reading or as structured records for programmatic use.

For the experiments in this paper only search is exercised.

---

## 4. Conversational Corpora as Documents

Applying a code index to conversation requires one decision: what is a document and what is a
section.

We treat each conversational session as a document and each turn within it as a section. The
transcript is written to markdown with a heading per turn, which the markdown extraction pass turns
into a section entity, exactly as it would for a documentation file. Session level metadata,
including the date, is written as front matter on the document and is therefore carried on every
section derived from it.

No conversational preprocessing occurs. There is no entity resolution, no coreference pass, no
temporal normalisation, no fact extraction. The corpus is the transcript.

This is worth stating plainly because it is the whole experiment. If a deterministic index over raw
transcripts is competitive with systems that spend hours of inference building structured
representations of the same transcripts, the structured representation is not doing the work people
assume it is doing.

---

## 5. A Retrieval Granularity Defect and Its Correction

### 5.1 One candidate per file

The candidate selection step admitted one unit per file. For code this is correct behaviour and
deliberate: a developer opening search results wants distinct files, not nine fragments of one
function.

For prose it is wrong. A document's heading regions already exist in the graph, are already scored,
and were then collapsed to a single representative. Measured on a real prose corpus at a retrieval
budget of 200, the shipped build returned **19 results across 19 files** while internally carrying
**195 additional regions holding 42 KB of evidence** that no consumer of the result array could
reach. Results ranked sixth and below received a single line of text.

### 5.2 Score collapse

An initial correction promoted the discarded regions into the unused portion of the result budget.
This helped, but incompletely, and the reason is instructive.

Promoted regions were **satellites**. Each inherited its parent's relevance score verbatim, and
promotions were ordered by a round robin over parent index and appended after every parent. The
consequence:

![Figure 1](figs/fig1_score_collapse.svg)

**Figure 1.** Distinct relevance scores among 200 returned results, by ranker configuration. The
shipped ranker and the satellite promotion variant both return 200 results carrying only 17.1
distinct scores on average; 181 of 200 results are score duplicates of one of 19 parents. Ranking
sections as first class candidates raises this to 84.9.

### 5.3 Why this starves multi-hop

A downstream consumer that sorts by relevance with a stable sort receives, from a payload carrying
19 distinct scores, **19 contiguous blocks**: one document's parent followed by all of its promoted
regions, then the next document's block, and so on.

Truncate that list to the first 50, 20, or 10 items and the consumer sees only the first one or two
documents.

Any question whose evidence must be assembled across documents therefore cannot be answered, not
because the retrieval missed the evidence, but because the ordering made it unreachable. This is a
structural impossibility rather than a probabilistic disadvantage, and it predicts exactly what we
measure: multi-hop was our worst category before the correction and improves most after it.

### 5.4 Section level candidates

The correction makes the prose retrieval unit the **section** rather than the file. A unit is keyed
by its heading's symbol identity, falling back to file path where a document has no section
structure. A section competes on its own score, exactly as an independent file would.

**Breadth is preserved by an explicit rule.** No document receives a second region until every
document that fits has received one. This rule binds every selection pass rather than only the
first. Without it, a document whose sections all score highly can crowd out a document holding the
single piece of evidence a question needs. We found this failure during development: a first
implementation that ranked sections purely by score dropped an entire document at small budgets, and
a corpus test caught it.

An off switch restores the previous behaviour, and its output is byte identical to the previous
build on every metric we measure. That identity is the cleanest available evidence that this change,
and nothing else, is responsible for the results reported here.

### 5.5 Effect on the returned payload

| configuration | items/q | distinct regions/q | distinct scores/q | files/q | visible chars/q |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| shipped ranker | 195.0 | 243.0 | 17.1 | 18.9 | 60,854 |
| satellite promotion | 195.0 | 243.0 | 17.1 | 18.9 | 60,854 |
| **section candidates** | **196.0** | **295.3** | **84.9** | **18.9** | **53,929** |
| off switch | 195.0 | 243.0 | 17.1 | 18.9 | 60,854 |

Score diversity rises fivefold. Document coverage is unchanged at 18.9 files per query, so section
diversity was not purchased with document coverage. **Bytes returned fall by 11.4%**, because the
previous build was computing regions and discarding them unread.

### 5.6 Code search is unaffected

Because the candidate selection step is shared between code and prose, this change is not
structurally inert for code the way a prose only pass would be. We therefore verified it.

Fifteen real locate queries against a 300,000 line Go repository, at retrieval budgets of 10 and 50,
comparing entire structured payloads including results, statistics, and diagnostics rather than
result lists alone: **30 of 30 payloads identical**.

Separately, we confirmed the prose gate cannot fire on a source repository even for documentation
flavoured queries. Three such queries returned zero results carrying the prose retrieval mode in
either build.

**Cost.** Prose search latency rises from 0.300 s to 0.628 s per query, because passages are planned
for roughly 196 units rather than 19. Code search latency is unchanged, since the prose path never
activates there.

---

## 6. Experimental Design

### 6.1 The measurement spine

Every arm shares the following. Deviating on any of these would make the comparison meaningless, so
a fairness guard exits on an asymmetric setting rather than warning.

| parameter | value |
|---|---|
| dataset | LoCoMo, all 1,540 questions, no subsetting |
| answerer | `gpt-5.6-sol`, identical for every arm |
| judge | `gpt-5.6-sol`, identical for every arm |
| retrieval budget | `top_k = 200` for every arm |
| ingest model, extraction arms | `azure_ai/gpt-5.6-terra` |
| ingest, entire-graph | none |
| scoring | run aggregate at the 200 cutoff, never a hand tallied subset |

The answerer and judge prompts are **byte identical to the upstream harness**. We did not author or
tune the grading.

### 6.2 Systems under test

Seven systems: entire-graph, mem0 open source, cognee, cmm, graphify, letta, and supermemory. Two
further systems appear as dashes. Graphiti did not complete: its ingest cost 4,463 seconds per
conversation and it reached three of ten with roughly 160 hours remaining. Mem0's managed tier is
not runnable under this spine because its answerer and judge cannot be pinned.

### 6.3 Gates

A run is void if dropped questions exceed 1%, or if empty context retrievals cluster by
conversation. Every published row has zero drops and zero empty context retrievals.

### 6.4 Same window measurement

The headline comparison ran entire-graph and mem0 **concurrently**, against the same endpoint, in
the same window, on the same questions.

This is not a formality. We measured **2.21 points of drift** on an identical entire-graph
configuration re-run 26 hours apart, with byte identical retrieval on 299 of 300 questions. That
drift exceeds the spread between the leading systems. Cross time comparison is not safe on this
harness, and we do not perform one for the headline.

Run to run noise is **0.65 points**: two identical mem0 configurations scored 93.83 and 93.57,
disagreeing on 11.3% of individual answers. Any margin below that threshold is not supportable,
including ours.

### 6.5 Instrumentation

Token measurement uses a transparent HTTP proxy in front of the shared extraction deployment. It
forwards method, path, query, body, and authentication verbatim and records only token accounting
from each response. No library is patched, so the measurement is identical across systems by
construction.

The proxy was validated against an independent meter inside mem0's own container. The two agreed
exactly on a single call and again across a full 419 chunk conversation: 419 calls, 3,605,747 prompt
tokens, identical on both instruments.

An earlier version of the proxy opened a fresh connection per request and exhibited failures under
concurrency, rising from 0% at two active arms to 56.2% at six. That defect was found by measuring
it, the proxy was rebuilt on a keep alive pool, and every figure reported here comes from the
rebuilt instrument at a verified 0% failure rate.

---

## 7. Results: Accuracy

All 1,540 questions, zero dropped questions in every row.

| # | system | LoCoMo | correct | ingest LLM calls |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **1** | **entire-graph** | **94.74** | 1459/1540 | **0** |
| 2 | mem0 OSS | 93.83 | 1445/1540 | 1 per chunk |
| 3 | cognee | 92.86 | 1430/1540 | 2 per chunk |
| 4 | cmm † | 91.30 | 1406/1540 | **0** |
| 5 | graphify | 87.34 | 1345/1540 | **0** |
| 6 | letta | 80.58 | 1241/1540 | agent controlled |
| 7 | supermemory ‡ | 77.60 | 1195/1540 | hosted |
| — | graphiti | did not complete | | |
| — | mem0 Pro | not runnable under this spine | | |

† cmm required a one line fix to its result filter to score at all. Its shipped build excludes its
own section nodes from both result queries, so a prose corpus returns an empty set. Reported in
cmm's favour. ‡ extraction model unverifiable, see Section 13.

### 7.1 The head to head

Against the same window mem0 control, on identical questions:

| category | entire-graph | mem0 | margin |
|---|---|---|---|
| overall | **94.74** | 93.83 | +0.91 |
| single-hop (841) | **96.67** | 95.12 | **+1.55**, p = 0.035 |
| multi-hop (282) | **93.97** | 93.62 | +0.35 |
| temporal (321) | **95.33** | 94.70 | +0.62 |
| open-domain (96) | 78.12 | **80.21** | −2.08 |

entire-graph leads three of four categories. Single-hop, which is 55% of the benchmark, is the one
cell that clears significance on its own.

The overall margin is +0.91 points with a discordant split of 43 to 29 and McNemar p = 0.125. We
report the ranking, which is what was measured, and decline to claim statistical significance for
the overall figure. We report the p-value and the noise floor because almost no paper in this
literature reports either, and a reader is entitled to both.

Against every system other than mem0 the margins run from 1.9 to 17.1 points and are well clear of
the noise floor.

---

## 8. Results: Retrieval Quality

Accuracy conflates retrieval with generation. Separating them produces the most surprising result in
the paper.

### 8.1 Answer generation is saturated

Across every system tested, **P(correct given gold evidence retrieved) is 0.96 to 0.97**.

The spread between systems lives almost entirely in retrieval. Supermemory's accuracy deficit is
approximately 90% attributable to retrieval failure, graphify's approximately 85%. This reframes
what the benchmark measures: on LoCoMo, with a strong reader, memory systems are being compared on
retrieval and almost nothing else.

### 8.2 Recall as the budget tightens

![Figure 3](figs/fig3_recall_at_k.svg)

**Figure 3.** Share of questions for which all gold evidence is recovered, as a function of the
retrieval cutoff. entire-graph recovers all gold evidence by rank 10 on 82.0% of questions, against
56.8% for graphify, 50.8% for supermemory, and 50.5% for cmm. mem0 and letta are omitted: they store
model rewritten facts with no verbatim overlap with the source, so evidence matching is not
identifiable for them rather than low.

| system | @10 | @20 | @50 | @200 | MRR |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **entire-graph** | **.820** | **.841** | — | .850 | .769 |
| graphify | .568 | .609 | .674 | .778 | .478 |
| supermemory | .508 | .570 | — | .648 | .397 |
| cmm | .505 | .577 | .682 | .858 | .418 |
| cognee | — | — | — | .899 | .960 |
| mem0, letta | not identifiable | | | | |

The 25 point gap at rank 10 is the largest separation anywhere in our results, and rank 10 is the
regime that matters when a context budget is tight.

Cognee's figure at 200 requires context: it returns **one unit containing 109% of the source
conversation**. It has no rank structure, so cutoff and reciprocal rank measures are undefined for
it, and its recall means "returns nearly everything" rather than "ranks well".

### 8.3 Where we are not first

Measured as gold items recovered per thousand characters returned, entire-graph is third:
supermemory .131, graphify .065, entire-graph .049, cmm .032, cognee .016.

Against mem0 the same picture holds at tight budgets. mem0 delivers roughly 43 accuracy points per
thousand characters at its narrowest cutoff against our 5.7, and wins at matched byte budgets below
roughly 25,000 characters. We deliver about 30% more context per question at the same nominal
retrieval budget, because our units are prose spans and theirs are distilled sentences.

This is a direct consequence of the zero inference design, and we report it because it is true and
because it is the most obvious attack on our accuracy result.

---

## 9. Results: Ingest Cost

Published work in this area reports wall clock, or reports nothing. These are measured token counts.

![Figure 2](figs/fig2_accuracy_vs_cost.svg)

**Figure 2.** LoCoMo accuracy against measured ingest cost. The shaded band holds the systems that
call no model at ingest. entire-graph occupies the top of that band. mem0 reaches 93.83 for 50.85
million tokens; cognee reaches 92.86 for 12.35 million. Letta and supermemory are omitted, the first
because its cost is not projectable and the second because it could not be metered; both are
explained below.

### 9.1 Per conversation

| mem0 | 0 | 419 | 419 | 1.000 | 3,605,747 | 38,748 | 8,698 |
| mem0 | 1 | 369 | 369 | 1.000 | 3,136,772 | 31,009 | 8,585 |

### 9.2 Full corpus

| system | LLM calls | tokens | basis |
|---|---|---|---|
| **entire-graph** | **0** | **0** | measured, by design |
| cmm, graphify | 0 | 0 | no model in the ingest path |
| cognee | 11,749 | **12.35M** | linear, conversations agree to 4.2% |
| mem0 | 5,882 | **50.85M** | linear, conversations agree to 1.3% |
| letta | not projectable | not projectable | see below |
| supermemory | not measurable | not measurable | Section 13 |

**Zero against 50.85 million, both measured.**

### 9.3 What the numbers show

**Linearity was tested rather than assumed.** mem0 is exactly 1.00 calls per chunk and cognee
exactly 2.00, across two conversations of different length. mem0's prompt size is flat across ingest
with quartile means of 8,492, 8,631, 8,656, and 8,643, which rules out the hypothesis that its cost
grows as the store fills.

**Letta is not projectable and we do not project it.** Its two conversations differ by 114.8% in
tokens per chunk, because its step count is chosen by its own agent loop rather than by the number
of chunks. A replicate confirmed this is a real property and not a truncation artifact: 52 calls
against the original 55. Per conversation figures are reliable; a corpus figure is not derivable
from them.

**Call count is not a proxy for cost.** Cognee makes twice mem0's calls and spends four times fewer
tokens, because mem0's prompt averages roughly 8,500 tokens per call against cognee's 750.

**Retries are counted.** Cognee logged client side timeouts on both conversations, and some of those
generations completed upstream and were billed. The totals are tokens actually consumed, because
that is what a provider bill reflects. Calls per chunk landed at 1.998 and 1.997 across conversations
with very different retry counts, which is what establishes 2.00 as cognee's real per chunk call
count rather than a retry artifact.

### 9.4 Wall clock, for completeness

Within the class that calls no model: entire-graph 7.0 s, cmm 4.3 s, graphify 5.9 s. Against
extraction based systems: letta 3,373 s, cognee 6,195 s, supermemory 15,379 s, mem0 20,478 s.

**The between class gap of roughly three orders of magnitude is the robust result.** The ordering
within the deterministic class spans 2.7 seconds and was measured on a shared machine, so we do not
treat it as established. We are not the fastest index to build; we are in the class that builds in
seconds rather than hours.

---

## 10. Ablations

Three configurations of the same system, on the same corpus, in the same window, differing only in
the binary.

![Figure 4](figs/fig4_ablation.svg)

**Figure 4.** Accuracy by question type across the three ranker configurations. Multi-hop, the
category the score collapse starved, gains 5.67 points across the two changes. Open-domain is the
one category where the second change does not help.

| configuration | overall | single-hop | multi-hop | temporal | open-domain |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| shipped ranker | 91.56 | 95.24 | 88.30 | 89.72 | 75.00 |
| + region promotion | 93.83 | 96.43 | 91.84 | 93.15 | 79.17 |
| **+ section candidates** | **94.74** | 96.67 | 93.97 | 95.33 | 78.12 |

The isolated effect of the first change, paired across all 1,540 questions with the binary as the
only variable, is **+2.27 points with a discordant split of 46 to 11 and McNemar p = 3.3e-06**. We
verified identical chunk counts, identical arguments, and identical corpus configuration on both
arms.

---

## 11. Analysis

### 11.1 Where the gains come from

Per loser forensics on every question mem0 answered correctly and we did not, before the correction,
produced a clean distribution: 56% retrieval miss, 28% synthesis failure, 9% rank burial, 6%
ambiguous gold, and no judge errors.

The mechanism behind the retrieval misses is specific. **entire-graph never failed to retrieve the
correct session**: the gold session appeared in 32 of 32 losses and 46 of 46 wins. What it missed
was the correct **turn** within that session, and **70% of missing gold turns sat within two turns
of a fragment already returned**.

That is the signature of a unit that is smaller than the unit of meaning. A single conversational
turn frequently opens with a pronoun whose referent lives in the preceding turn. One loss turned on
a turn reading "maybe we can try it together sometime", where the subject appeared only in the turn
before, which was not retrieved.

### 11.2 A remedy we built and rejected

The obvious response is to expand each retrieved fragment into its neighbours, paying for the
expansion by deduplicating text already returned. We implemented it, and we do not ship it.

Measured across all 32 losing questions against an unchanged control: gold evidence turns recovered
rose from 21 of 51 to 23 of 51. Two turns, both inside a single question. **One conversion in 32.**
Per question bytes were non increasing throughout, so the change was genuinely budget neutral. It
simply does not buy enough.

An earlier build of the same change appeared to convert five questions. It also grew the text handed
to the reader by 90%. Its byte ceiling had been placed on the serialised payload rather than on
snippet text, and because the structural envelope of a result dwarfs a prose snippet, discarding
duplicate results freed envelope that does not exist as text. Re-bounded on the text a reader
actually sees, the gain vanished. We record this because the failure mode, bounding an expansion on
the wrong meter, produces a result that looks rigorous and is not.

### 11.3 Why open-domain resists

Open-domain is our one losing category and the weakest category for every system tested, at 65 to 81
points against 92 to 97 on single-hop. Reading all 96 questions explains why. Roughly a dozen are not
answerable from the transcript by any system: the gold answer is one annotator's choice among many
valid ones, or requires world knowledge keyed on a detail, or the question asks about an absence and
has no evidence turns at all. On many of these both systems produce the same answer and both are
marked wrong.

The gap between us and mem0 on this category is four questions out of 96, against a benchmark where
two identical mem0 runs disagree with each other on eight of those same 96. We do not treat it as a
real difference, and we would need roughly 470 open-domain questions to resolve one of this size.

---

## 12. Threats to Validity

We list these in full because the campaign that produced this paper withdrew five of its own claims,
and a reader should be able to see which survived.

### 12.1 Answer key defects

An independent audit of LoCoMo reports 99 score corrupting ground truth errors, 6.4% of the
benchmark, implying a ceiling near 93.6% for a perfect system, which is below both leading scores.

We verified the audit rather than assuming or dismissing it. Its dataset copy is byte identical to
the upstream release, its per category counts match ours exactly, and we independently confirmed 12
of 12 spot checked errors against raw transcripts across the hallucination, temporal, and attribution
classes. We treat the 99 as real.

Re-scoring four ways:

| treatment | entire-graph | mem0 | margin |
|---|---|---|---|
| as published | 94.74 | 93.83 | +0.91 |
| all 99 removed | 96.39 | 95.35 | +1.04 |
| per item corrected key | 94.48 | 93.51 | +0.97 |
| every disputed credit void | 90.19 | 89.22 | +0.97 |

**The margin widens under every treatment.** The defective questions are neutral between the arms:
entire-graph takes 70 of 99 and mem0 takes 71, with exact p = 1.000.

The audit's ceiling assumes a perfect system is penalised on all 99. Our data shows that premise is
too strong. Adjudicating each disputed item individually, only 4 of our 70 credits are genuine false
credit; 62 of 70 are answers matching the audit's own corrected answer rather than the defective
gold. There are also 12 to 16 false debits in the other direction.

### 12.2 Judge behaviour

Hand adjudication of 60 correct marked answers found entire-graph at 30 of 30 genuine matches with
zero lenient credits. The one clear and one borderline over credit both fell in the mem0 control arm.

Two systematic tolerances exist in the upstream prompt and apply symmetrically: a duration tolerance
of roughly plus or minus 50%, and recall only grading of list answers, which forgives both supersets
and partial subsets.

### 12.3 Loader deviation

Our loader ingests the dataset's image captions and annotator query fields; the reference loader does
not. 18 of 1,540 gold answers, 1.17%, contain content recoverable only from the query field, and a
further 36 only from captions. This is symmetric across arms and does not affect the comparison, but
**our absolute scores are not comparable to publications using a text only loader**, and it partly
explains why both leading arms exceed the audited ceiling.

### 12.4 Context volume is not equalised by the retrieval budget

The retrieval budget equalises item count, not text volume. We deliver roughly 30% more context per
question than mem0 at the same nominal budget. At tight cutoffs the disparity is far larger, up to
7.9 times, which is why we exclude cutoff comparisons entirely.

### 12.5 Scope

All results are LoCoMo with one answerer and one judge model. Generality across benchmarks and model
families is not established here. The graphify and cmm adapters were written by us, and a vendor
implementation might perform better.

---

## 13. Competitor Defects and Provenance

### 13.1 Three defects we fixed in the competitors' favour

| system | defect | effect |
|---|---|---|
| mem0 | the adapter passed a `limit` argument to a signature expecting `top_k`, so it was absorbed into keyword arguments and every search silently returned 20 memories instead of 200 | **+6.04** |
| cognee | state persisted to disk while the retrieval buffer lived in memory, so a resumed run searched nothing and answered confidently | **+13.77** |
| cmm | the shipped BM25 path excludes its own section node type from both result queries, so a prose corpus returns an empty result set | **structurally zero to 91.30** |

A fourth, in mem0, we disclose rather than repair: its stored timestamps reflect ingestion time
rather than conversation time, because backdating is a paid tier capability that raises an error in
the open source build. Measured effect on its score: two answers in 1,540, 0.13 points.

### 13.2 A defect in our own harness

A hardcoded 15 second connection timeout, combined with unjittered backoff, caused the first call of
every worker thread to fail during a cold start, scoring correct answers as wrong. The configured
timeout applied only to reads, never to connection establishment. Cost: 10 questions per run, 0.65
points, **larger than the effect under study**. Fixed in shared code and verified from 10 empty
answers to 0 on two backends.

### 13.3 One row whose provenance we cannot establish

Supermemory's extraction model cannot be determined from surviving records, and this is our failure
rather than the vendor's.

It was **not** the mock: during the run window, zero files were written in the mock backed store
while 23,536 were written in the store the run actually used, and extraction latencies cluster at 13
to 32 seconds against a mock's sub 10 milliseconds.

The canonical extraction model is **very likely impossible** for it. Probing the shared deployment
parameter by parameter, it rejects six parameters that supermemory's server emits, and 143 of its
calls returned errors even after a compatibility shim. It cannot call that deployment without
substantial request rewriting, which is also why we could not meter its ingest cost without ceasing
to forward requests unchanged.

Which model it did use is unrecoverable. Environment capture tooling was created six hours after the
run completed, no shell history survives, and the harness does not log upstream host or model for any
arm.

**We retain the row with this disclosure rather than present it as a same extractor comparison, and
we read 77.60 as a lower bound on supermemory rather than a measurement of it.** Independently, 221
of its 1,540 questions returned zero memories, with normal retrieval latency, so these are genuine
misses rather than a buffer defect.

### 13.4 What we should have done

This provenance gap exists because we did not capture our benchmark runs with session recording,
which would have committed model, endpoint, environment, and arguments automatically at the time of
the run. Every subsequent campaign should. We record the omission rather than presenting the run as
better attributed than it is.

---

## 14. Reproducibility

Everything in this paper is reproducible from `bench/memory/` in the entire-graph repository.

The kit contains the entire-graph adapter, the competitor ports we wrote, the fairness
specification, a run index mapping every quoted number to a stored artifact, and four apply checked
patches for the upstream files we modified. The upstream fork point is pinned by **md5 verified byte
comparison** rather than a recorded commit hash, and the answerer and judge prompts are byte
identical to upstream.

Every score was recomputed from raw per question artifacts by two independent methods sharing no
code, agreeing to the last digit.

---

## 15. Limitations and Future Work

**Static analysis is incomplete by construction.** Dynamic dispatch, dependency injection, runtime
registration, decorators, and code generation all produce relations no parser recovers. On prose this
matters less, but on code it bounds what the index can know.

**Single benchmark.** LoCoMo alone, one answerer, one judge. LongMemEval and a second reader family
are the obvious next requirements, and we regard the present result as evidence rather than proof.

**Context efficiency is our real weakness.** Closing it means shorter retrieval units, which means
distillation, which means inference at ingest. That trade should be made deliberately if it is made
at all, because zero inference is the property that distinguishes this system.

**The interesting open question is the amortisation frontier.** At what ratio of reads to writes does
paying a model at index time earn back its cost? We have measured both axes for one corpus. The
general form of that curve is, as far as we can determine, unformalised, and it is the question this
work most naturally leads to.

---

## 16. Conclusion

A deterministic structural index built for source code, applied unchanged to conversational
transcripts, places first among seven memory systems on LoCoMo. It scores above the strongest open
source competitor by 0.91 points, a margin we report without a significance claim, and above the
remaining five by 1.9 to 17.1 points. It recovers all gold evidence by rank 10 on 82.0% of questions
against 56.8% for the next measurable system.

It does this at a measured ingest cost of **zero language model calls and zero tokens**, against
mem0's measured 5,882 calls and 50.85 million tokens and cognee's 11,749 calls and 12.35 million
tokens for the same corpus.

That comparison is the clearest result here. It is the only one not subject to a statistical tie, and
it is the one that compounds, because extraction cost recurs on every document change and zero does
not.

On this benchmark, with a strong reader, the extraction step does not buy accuracy. It buys context
efficiency, which is a real advantage at tight budgets and which we report against ourselves. Whether
that trade is worth three orders of magnitude in index construction cost depends on how often the
corpus changes, and we suggest the field should measure that ratio rather than assume it.

Reproduction protocol · LoCoMo · n = 1540

Running LoCoMo yourself

Everything needed to independently re-run the memory-system comparison, including the five settings that silently produce wrong numbers if you get them wrong. We got each of them wrong at least once.

What you are running

LoCoMo is a long-conversation question-answering benchmark: ten multi-session conversations, 1,540 questions across four types. A memory system ingests the conversations, then for each question returns the evidence it thinks is relevant. A reader model answers from that evidence and a judge model scores the answer.

The benchmark measures retrieval, not memory architecture. Across every system we tested, the probability of a correct answer given that the gold evidence was retrieved is 0.96 to 0.97. The reader is saturated. Almost all of the spread between systems is in what came back from search().

Before you start

  • An OpenAI-compatible chat endpoint you can point at, with a deployment for the reader/judge model and one for any extraction model your arms use. We used Azure AI.
  • Roughly 2 to 3 hours per arm for the question phase at the settings below.
  • Ingest time varies enormously by system: seconds for a deterministic index, and up to 5.7 hours for an LLM-extraction system on this corpus.
  • Disk. Some arms hold multiple gigabytes of state.

The spine

These are the settings every arm must share. If any of them differs between two arms, those two numbers cannot be compared, and no amount of care elsewhere fixes it.

scoringthe run's own aggregate, never a hand-summed subset

Why ingest is not equalised

A deterministic index calls no model at ingest; an extraction system calls one per chunk. That asymmetry is the thing being measured. Forcing them to match would erase the result. It is disclosed in the output, not homogenised away.

The run

01

Get the upstream harness at a pinned commit

git clone https://github.com/mem0ai/memory-benchmarks.git
cd memory-benchmarks
git checkout 4b61c5d31b9c

Pin it. The harness changes, and a floating checkout means your numbers and ours were produced by different code.

02

Apply the patches

for p in bench/memory/patches/000[1-4]-*.patch; do
  git apply -p1 "$p"
done

Four upstream files are modified: provider timeouts, optional date injection, retry and drop accounting, and a server-side fix. Each patch is apply-checked against the pinned commit. Everything else is unmodified upstream code, including the reader and judge prompts.

03

Copy in the adapters

cp -r bench/memory/benchmarks/common/*.py benchmarks/common/

New files only. These are the per-system adapters and the fairness guard. No upstream source is touched by this step.

04

Export credentials by name

export AZURE_AI_ENDPOINT=...
export AZURE_AI_API_VERSION=2024-05-01-preview

The launcher refuses to start without these. Never commit the values, and prefer a key you can rotate afterwards.

05

Run one arm

bash bench/memory/run_locomo.sh cmm

One arm at a time, or at most three concurrently. The launcher refuses to start a second copy of the same arm, which is a guard we added after two processes on one project name destroyed a run.

Five things that silently produce wrong numbers

Each of these produced a plausible-looking result that was simply false. None of them raised an error at the time.

1 · The default concurrency

The harness defaults to 100 question-workers at 200 requests per minute. Against a shared deployment that is roughly 300 concurrent requests, which saturates the endpoint so thoroughly that almost every call times out and retries.

Use --max-workers 3 --question-workers 10 --rpm 60 with LLM_TIMEOUT=600. Fewer, more patient requests finish dramatically faster. One arm went from zero questions in ten minutes to 660 in eighteen.

2 · State roots under /tmp

The default temporary directory resolves under /tmp, which systemd wipes on boot. Multi-gigabyte arm state disappeared this way.

Put state roots under $HOME. The launcher does this, but check it if you adapt the script.

3 · Resuming into an empty buffer

Several clients write ingest checkpoints to disk while holding the retrieval buffer in memory. A resumed run sees the checkpoints, skips ingest, and then searches nothing, answering every question confidently from an empty context.

This destroyed one system's score by 13.77 points before we found it. Make search() raise on a missing buffer rather than return an empty list, and treat zero-context questions clustered by conversation as a void run.

4 · Connect timeouts, not read timeouts

LLM_TIMEOUT sets the read timeout. The connect timeout is separate and was hardcoded at 15 seconds. Every worker's first call opens a fresh connection simultaneously; on a NAT'd host those handshakes are dropped and every one of them fails at exactly 15.02 seconds. Unjittered backoff then keeps the whole group synchronised through all five retries.

Cost: ten questions per run scored wrong, worth 0.65 points, which was larger than the effect we were trying to measure. Raise the connect timeout and jitter the backoff.

5 · Comparing runs from different windows

We re-ran an identical configuration 26 hours apart and got results 2.21 points apart, with byte-identical retrieval on 299 of 300 questions. The systems had not changed; the endpoint's behaviour had.

Run the arms you intend to compare concurrently. Two identical runs of one system differ by 0.65 points and disagree on 11.3% of individual answers, so treat that as your noise floor and distrust any margin under it.

Is your run valid?

Check these before reading the score. A run that fails any of them is void, and dropping it is cheaper than explaining it later.

  • Dropped questions under 1%, and dropped symmetrically across arms.
  • No zero-context retrievals, and specifically none clustered by conversation, which is the signature of trap 3.
  • No empty generated answers. A cluster of them at the start of a run is trap 4.
  • One process per project name. Two processes sharing checkpoints will silently corrupt each other.
  • Read the score from the run's own aggregate, not from a re-derivation.

Sanity check on any competitor

A system scoring near zero is a broken integration until proven otherwise. Three of the six systems we measured were suppressed by defects in their own shipped code, worth +6.04, +13.77, and one that returned no results on prose at all. Diagnose before publishing.

Deterministic Structural Retrieval for Conversational Memory:
A Zero-Inference Index at the Top of LoCoMo

entire-graph project

Entire

Artifacts: entireio/entire-graph, bench/memory/ (PR #104)

Abstract—Agent memory systems almost universally construct their index by invoking a language model over every stored item. The cost is large, it recurs on every update, and it has not been shown to be necessary. We evaluate entire-graph, a deterministic structural index that performs zero language model calls at ingest, against six memory systems on LoCoMo under a single shared answerer and judge. entire-graph places first at 94.74 % across all 1,540 questions, above mem0 (93.83 %), cognee (92.86 %), cmm (91.30 %), graphify (87.34 %), letta (80.58 %) and supermemory (77.60 %). The margin over mem0 is 0.91 points at p = 0.125; we report the ranking and decline to claim significance for it. On retrieval quality the separation is larger: entire-graph recovers all gold evidence by rank 10 on 82.0 % of questions against 56.8 % for the next measurable system. We further report the first directly metered ingest-cost comparison in this literature: 0 calls and 0 tokens against mem0's 5,882 calls and 50.85 M tokens and cognee's 11,749 calls and 12.35 M tokens, with mem0's figure independently confirmed by its own internal meter. Finally we report a defect in our own ranker that suppressed our score by 3.18 points, its mechanism, and its correction.

Index Terms—retrieval, agent memory, code intelligence, static analysis, benchmark reproducibility, empirical software engineering.

I. Introduction

A memory system for a language agent solves a narrow problem. Given a corpus larger than the context window and a question, return the evidence that answers it.

The dominant design answers this by paying a language model to read the corpus at ingest, extract facts or assemble a graph, and store the result [1], [2], [3]. The appeal is clear: a model normalises phrasing, resolves pronouns, and infers relations no parser recovers.

The cost profile is less often stated. The extraction bill is not paid once. It is paid again for every document that changes, every session appended, every correction applied. For a corpus under active revision, which describes a codebase, a wiki, a ticket system, or an ongoing conversation, ingest cost does not amortise.

The alternative is a deterministic index: parse with a grammar, build a structure, rank with lexical and structural signals, call no model. This is mature technology in program analysis [4], [5], [6], where it has been standard for over a decade. It is not what agent memory systems do.

This paper asks whether the extraction step buys anything on a standard conversational memory benchmark, and answers with measurements.

A. Contributions

A deterministic index leads the LoCoMo table with zero inference at ingest. Its margin over the strongest open-source competitor is reported without a significance claim; its margin over the remaining five ranges from 1.9 to 17.1 points.

Retrieval quality separates more cleanly than accuracy. entire-graph recovers all gold evidence by rank 10 on 82.0 % of questions against 56.8 % for the next measurable system, a 25-point gap on the metric governing behaviour under a constrained budget.

We report the first directly metered ingest-cost comparison in this literature, cross-validated against a competitor's own instrumentation with exact agreement.

We report a retrieval-granularity defect in our own system, its mechanism, and its correction, worth 3.18 points at 11.4 % fewer returned bytes.

We disclose four competitor defects we repaired in the competitors' favour, five claims of our own that we withdrew, and one published row whose provenance we could not establish.

II. Related Work

A. Agent memory

Mem0 [1] extracts and consolidates facts with a language model and reports cost and latency advantages over full-context stuffing rather than accuracy advantages. Zep and Graphiti [2] build temporal knowledge graphs. Cognee runs a multi-stage pipeline per chunk. Letta [3] maintains archival passages under agent control. A-MEM [7] and HippoRAG 2 [8] construct associative structures over extracted units. LightMem [9] reports large online token reductions with accuracy gains. Every one of these performs inference at ingest, and most per stored item.

A recent line questions whether that inference is load-bearing. DMF [10] reports deterministic memory at comparable accuracy with large token reductions. Zero-Mem [11] reports a memory path invoking no model outside final answering. ReFind [12] reports that a lexical interface over the unmodified archive, building no semantic structure, tops MemoryAgentBench. Our result is consistent with that direction. What distinguishes it is the index: ours was built for source code and is applied to conversation unchanged.

B. Deterministic code intelligence

Structural indexes over source are mature. Code property graphs [4] unify syntax, control flow and data dependence. CodeQL [5] exposes a relational query language over an extracted database. Stack graphs [6] resolve names incrementally at scale. Kythe, Glean, SCIP and LSIF are industrial expressions of the same idea. None calls a model; all are deterministic given a commit.

A recent wave wraps such indexes for agents: RepoGraph [13], CodexGraph [14], LocAgent [15], CGM [16] and GraphCoder [17]. entire-graph belongs to this family by construction. Its contribution here is not the index, which is conventional, but the demonstration that a conventional code index is competitive in a domain the code-intelligence literature does not address and the memory literature does not draw from. We note that lexical retrieval has recently been shown competitive with graph baselines for repository-level completion [18], a result our own code-side measurements do not contradict.

C. Retrieval granularity

Dense X Retrieval [19] establishes that finer retrieval units outperform passage units, and that the advantage widens under a fixed context budget. RAPTOR [20] builds a hierarchical summary tree. Parent-document retrieval is standard practice. The correction in Section V is an instance of this established principle rather than a new technique. We report it because the failure mode it corrects, score collapse under per-document deduplication, does not appear to have been named, and because its magnitude here is large enough that publishing our score without the mechanism would be uninterpretable.

III. The entire-graph Index

A. Design constraints

No inference. No model is called during index construction. There is no extraction pass, no model-computed embedding, no summarisation. Construction is parsing plus graph assembly.

Determinism. The same commit yields a byte-identical index. This is what allows the system to serve as a measurement instrument, since it cannot drift between runs, and it is a property no sampling-based extraction pipeline offers.

No egress. Construction and query are local. There is no network path in either.

B. Symbol and relation layers

Files are parsed with tree-sitter grammars. Each grammar contributes an extraction pass emitting symbol entities: functions, methods, classes, types, constants, routes, and for prose formats, document sections. Every symbol carries a content-derived identity, a kind, a qualified name, a source range, a signature where one exists, its language and its container. Identity is not positional, so edits elsewhere in a file do not renumber unrelated symbols.

For markdown the extraction pass emits one section entity per heading. A transcript stored as markdown therefore yields a section per turn. This is the same machinery that yields a function per declaration in Go; nothing about the prose path is special-cased.

Relations are emitted between symbols and between symbols and external endpoints: calls, inheritance and interface satisfaction, field access, type usage, imports, route handling and containment. Each carries a resolution status and confidence. Unresolved endpoints are retained rather than dropped. Relation extraction is static and therefore incomplete by construction; dynamic dispatch, reflection, runtime registration and code generation all produce edges no parser recovers. We treat this as a stated limitation.

C. Ranking and budgeting

A query is scored by a hybrid function combining lexical match over bodies and identifiers with case-aware tokenisation, signature and qualified-name match, path and container signals, and graph proximity to matched symbols. A candidate-selection step then decides which units are eligible, and a byte-fitting step assembles snippets under a context budget.

The budget is enforced during assembly rather than after. When a pass expands or rewrites spans, the ceiling is computed before the pass runs and each expansion is committed individually and reverted if it would breach the ceiling. Post-pass text can therefore never exceed pre-pass text. This property is what permits the claim in Section V that the reported improvement is not purchased with a larger prompt.

D. Prose corpora

Prose corpora are detected rather than declared. A corpus is treated as prose when it contains at least four units and at least 80 % of its paths carry document extensions. Below that threshold the prose path does not activate and the ranker behaves as it does for code. This gate is why the change in Section V is inert on a source repository, a claim we verify empirically in Section V-F.

Applying the index to conversation requires one decision: what is a document and what is a section. We treat each session as a document and each turn as a section, written to markdown with a heading per turn and session metadata as front matter. No conversational preprocessing occurs: no entity resolution, no coreference pass, no temporal normalisation, no fact extraction. The corpus is the transcript. This is the whole experiment. If a deterministic index over raw transcripts is competitive with systems spending hours of inference building structured representations of the same transcripts, the structured representation is not doing the work it is assumed to do.

IV. Experimental Design

A. The measurement spine

Every arm shares the parameters in Table I. Deviating on any of them would make the comparison meaningless, so a fairness guard exits on an asymmetric setting rather than warning. The answerer and judge prompts are byte-identical to the upstream harness; we did not author or tune the grading.

B. Gates and windows

A run is void if dropped questions exceed 1 %, or if empty-context retrievals cluster by conversation. Every published row has zero of both.

The headline comparison ran entire-graph and mem0 concurrently, against the same endpoint, in the same window, on the same questions. This is not a formality. We measured 2.21 points of drift on an identical entire-graph configuration re-run 26 hours apart, with byte-identical retrieval on 299 of 300 questions. That drift exceeds the spread between leading systems.

Run-to-run noise is 0.65 points: two identical mem0 configurations scored 93.83 and 93.57, disagreeing on 11.3 % of individual answers. Any margin below that threshold is not supportable, including ours.

C. Instrumentation

Token measurement uses a transparent HTTP proxy in front of the shared extraction deployment, forwarding requests verbatim and recording only token accounting. No library is patched, so the measurement is identical across systems by construction. The proxy was validated against an independent meter inside mem0's container: the two agreed exactly on a single call and again across a full 419-chunk conversation.

An earlier proxy opened a fresh connection per request and failed under concurrency, from 0 % at two active arms to 56.2 % at six. That defect was found by measuring it; every figure reported here comes from the rebuilt instrument at a verified 0 % failure rate.

V. A Retrieval-Granularity Defect

A. One candidate per file

The candidate-selection step admitted one unit per file. For code this is deliberate and correct: a developer wants distinct files, not nine fragments of one function. For prose it is wrong. A document's heading regions already exist in the graph, are already scored, and were then collapsed to a single representative. At a budget of 200 the shipped build returned 19 results across 19 files while internally carrying 195 additional regions holding 42 KB of evidence no consumer of the result array could reach.

B. Score collapse

An initial correction promoted the discarded regions into the unused budget. It helped incompletely, and the reason is instructive. Promoted regions were satellites: each inherited its parent's score verbatim, ordered by round-robin over parent index and appended after every parent.

C. Why this starves multi-hop

A consumer sorting by relevance with a stable sort receives, from a payload carrying 19 distinct scores, 19 contiguous blocks: one document's parent followed by its promoted regions, then the next. Truncated to the first 50, 20 or 10 items, the consumer sees only the first one or two documents. Any question whose evidence must be assembled across documents therefore cannot be answered, not because retrieval missed it, but because the ordering made it unreachable. This is a structural impossibility rather than a probabilistic disadvantage, and it predicts what we measure: multi-hop was the worst category before the correction and improves most after it.

D. Section-level candidates

The correction makes the prose retrieval unit the section rather than the file, keyed by the heading's symbol identity and falling back to file path where a document has no section structure. A section competes on its own score, exactly as an independent file would.

Breadth is preserved by an explicit rule: no document receives a second region until every document that fits has received one, binding every selection pass rather than only the first. Without it, a document whose sections all score highly crowds out a document holding the single piece of evidence a question needs. We encountered this during development; a corpus test caught it.

An off switch restores the previous behaviour, and its output is byte-identical to the previous build on every metric. That identity is the cleanest evidence that this change alone is responsible for the results reported here.

E. Effect on the payload

F. Code search is unaffected

Because candidate selection is shared between code and prose, this change is not structurally inert for code. We therefore verified it. Fifteen locate queries against a 300,000-line Go repository, at budgets of 10 and 50, comparing entire structured payloads including statistics and diagnostics rather than result lists alone: 30 of 30 payloads identical. Separately, three documentation-flavoured queries confirmed the prose gate cannot fire on a source repository.

Prose search latency rises from 0.300 s to 0.628 s per query, since passages are planned for roughly 196 units rather than 19. Code-search latency is unchanged.

VI. Results

A. Accuracy

Against the same-window mem0 control, entire-graph leads three of four categories: single-hop 96.67 against 95.12 (p = 0.035), multi-hop 93.97 against 93.62, temporal 95.33 against 94.70, and open-domain 78.12 against 80.21. Single-hop, 55 % of the benchmark, is the one cell clearing significance alone.

The overall margin is 0.91 points with a discordant split of 43 to 29 and McNemar p = 0.125. We report the ranking, which is what was measured, and decline to claim statistical significance for the overall figure. We report the p-value and the noise floor because almost no work in this literature reports either.

B. Retrieval quality

Accuracy conflates retrieval with generation. Separating them produces the most surprising result here: across every system tested, the probability of a correct answer given that gold evidence was retrieved is 0.96 to 0.97. The reader is saturated, and the spread between systems lives almost entirely in retrieval. Supermemory's deficit is roughly 90 % attributable to retrieval failure, graphify's roughly 85 %.

Cognee's figure at 200 requires context: it returns one unit containing 109 % of the source conversation, so cutoff and reciprocal-rank measures are undefined for it and its recall means "returns nearly everything" rather than "ranks well".

Measured as gold items per thousand characters returned, entire-graph is third at 0.049, behind supermemory at 0.131 and graphify at 0.065. Against mem0 the same picture holds at tight budgets: mem0 delivers roughly 43 accuracy points per thousand characters at its narrowest cutoff against our 5.7, and wins at matched byte budgets below roughly 25,000 characters. We deliver about 30 % more context at the same nominal budget, a direct consequence of the zero-inference design. We report it because it is the most obvious attack on our accuracy result.

Letta is not projectable and we do not project it: its step count is chosen by its own agent loop rather than by chunk count, and a replicate confirmed this is a real property rather than a truncation artifact.

Call count is not a proxy for cost. Cognee makes twice mem0's calls and spends four times fewer tokens, because mem0's prompt averages roughly 8,500 tokens per call against cognee's 750. Retries are counted, since that is what a provider bill reflects.

The between-class gap of roughly three orders of magnitude is the robust result. The ordering within the deterministic class spans 2.7 s on a shared machine and we do not treat it as established: we are not the fastest index to build, we are in the class that builds in seconds rather than hours.

D. Ablation

The isolated effect of the first change, paired across all 1,540 questions with the binary as the only variable, is 2.27 points with a discordant split of 46 to 11 and McNemar p = 3.3 × 10−6. We verified identical chunk counts, arguments and corpus configuration on both arms.

VII. Analysis

A. Where the gains come from

Per-loser forensics on every question mem0 answered correctly and we did not, before the correction, gave a clean distribution: 56 % retrieval miss, 28 % synthesis failure, 9 % rank burial, 6 % ambiguous gold, and no judge errors.

The mechanism is specific. entire-graph never failed to retrieve the correct session: the gold session appeared in 32 of 32 losses and 46 of 46 wins. What it missed was the correct turn, and 70 % of missing gold turns sat within two turns of a fragment already returned. That is the signature of a retrieval unit smaller than the unit of meaning. A conversational turn frequently opens with a pronoun whose referent lives in the preceding turn.

B. A remedy we built and rejected

The obvious response is to expand each fragment into its neighbours, paying for it by deduplicating text already returned. We implemented it and do not ship it. Across all 32 losing questions against an unchanged control, gold turns recovered rose from 21 of 51 to 23 of 51: two turns, both inside a single question, one conversion in 32, with per-question bytes non-increasing throughout.

An earlier build of the same change appeared to convert five questions while growing the text handed to the reader by 90 %. Its byte ceiling had been placed on the serialised payload rather than on snippet text, and because the structural envelope of a result dwarfs a prose snippet, discarding duplicates freed envelope that does not exist as text. Re-bounded on the text a reader sees, the gain vanished. We record this because the failure mode, bounding an expansion on the wrong meter, produces a result that looks rigorous and is not.

VIII. Threats to Validity

A. Answer-key defects

An independent audit of LoCoMo reports 99 score-corrupting ground-truth errors, 6.4 % of the benchmark, implying a ceiling near 93.6 % for a perfect system, below both leading scores. We verified rather than assumed: the audit's dataset copy is byte-identical to the upstream release, its per-category counts match ours exactly, and we independently confirmed 12 of 12 spot-checked errors against raw transcripts.

Table V. Re-scoring under answer-key correction
